messages.author: badb3818cf6ba1fe
messages.subject: Stan's approach for hierarchical models
parts:
Hi

I have a couple of questions regarding Stan's (NUTS/HMC_DA) approach to hierarchical models. This is just to further my understanding of how Stan works. 

Question 1.

Consider a simple hierarchical regresson, where i stands for individuals and j for observations belonging to an individual. 


y_{ij} = x_{ij} \beta_{i} + e_{ij}, j=1 to n_{i}, i=1 to I,   \beta_{i} is a vector of coefficients for individual i.  

\beta_{i} ~ N(\mu, \Lambda), where mu_{i} is the population mean and \Lambda is a variance covariance matrix. 

e_{ij} ~ N(0, \sigma^{2}), where \sigma^{2} is a univariate variance parameter. 

In Gibbs sampling (or MH sampling within Gibbs in non-conjugate cases) one works from blocks of parameters, { \beta_{i} }, \mu, \Lambda and \sigma^{2}. 

Does HMC_DA or NUTS use an underlying blocking scheme based on the conditional independence structure of the DAG  to reject or accept on a given iteration? That is, does it accept or reject the \beta_{i} for each individual separately, or are the entire set of parameters (individual level and population parameters) accepted or rejected in one go? What are the pros and cons of doing it in one go? 

Question 2. 

How does Stan handle different variable scales. It appears that a different epsilon is being used for each parameter.  How does this modify the HMC algorithms in the NUTS paper by Hoffman and Gelman? Is there some place where this is documented?

Thanks 

Asim

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Stan's approach for hierarchical models
parts:
On 1/9/13 1:11 PM, Asim wrote:
> Hi
>
> I have a couple of questions regarding Stan's (NUTS/HMC_DA) approach to hierarchical models. This is just to further my
> understanding of how Stan works.
>
> Question 1.
>
> Consider a simple hierarchical regresson, where i stands for individuals and j for observations belonging to an individual.
>
>
> y_{ij} = x_{ij} \beta_{i} + e_{ij}, j=1 to n_{i}, i=1 to I, \beta_{i} is a vector of coefficients for individual i.
>
> \beta_{i} ~ N(\mu, \Lambda), where mu_{i} is the population mean and \Lambda is a variance covariance matrix.
>
> e_{ij} ~ N(0, \sigma^{2}), where \sigma^{2} is a univariate variance parameter.
>
> In Gibbs sampling (or MH sampling within Gibbs in non-conjugate cases) one works from blocks of parameters, { \beta_{i}
> }, \mu, \Lambda and \sigma^{2}.

There are many ways to implement Gibbs.

You can do it blockwise or variable-at-a-time. And
there are lots of choices for sampling in non-conjugate
cases -- BUGS and JAGS make slightly different choices,
but in no case do they fall back to random-walk
Metropolis in multiple dimensions (except insofar as
you can think of Gibbs as a Metropolis method with
a 100% accept probabilty).

I believe BUGS/JAGS do a single variable at a time, which is
a block of 1 for most variables and a block of N for
a size N multivariate type (such as a simplex or covariance
matrix). JAGS adds some extra intelligence for sufficient
statistics for GLMs, I think.

> Does HMC_DA or NUTS use an underlying blocking scheme based on the conditional independence structure of the DAG to
> reject or accept on a given iteration?

I'm not sure what you mean by HMC_DA. Basic HMC is well
described in Radford Neal's handbook chapter, available here:

http://www.mcmchandbook.net/HandbookSampleChapters.html

HMC, like Gibbs or Metropolis, can be blocked. Just hold a
subset of the parameters constant and run the dynamics on the rest.

This can be particularly beneficial for hierarchical models where
you have reasonable conditional independence or where you can
use exact Gibbs updates for some of the parameters. Neal discusses
examples.

Stan doesn't do any blocking yet. Also, Stan does NOT assume
an underlying directed acyclic graphical model structure. All
we need to have is a definition of the (log) posterior probability
density up to a proportion. We then follow that function's gradient,
not an underlying graph structure.

> That is, does it accept or reject the \beta_{i} for each individual separately,
> or are the entire set of parameters (individual level and population parameters) accepted or rejected in one go? What
> are the pros and cons of doing it in one go?

It's all done in one go in Stan now. See Radford's paper, which
has a fair bit of discussion. The issues are mainly with scaling,
rotation, and varying curvature by position:

> Question 2.
>
> How does Stan handle different variable scales. It appears that a different epsilon is being used for each parameter.

Right. There's a discussion in Neal's handbook about
different ways to formulate it, and we're going with
varying step sizes in Stan.

Having said that, Yuanjun Gao just finished a global
(non-diagonal) mass matrix adaptation that will allow
some curvature, and that's implemented as a mass matrix.
Again, see Neal's paper.

And in a couple months, we hope to have a full Riemann
Manifold HMC implementation, which uses a very different
(position dependent) technique to deal with rotation and scaling
that's more computationally intensive but can be much
faster to converge and mix after convergence.

> How does this modify the HMC algorithms in the NUTS paper by Hoffman and Gelman? Is there some place where this is
> documented?

There's no place it's all cleanly documented in simple algorithmic
form that would make it easy to reproduce. And the Gelman and
Hoffman paper don't have detailed specifics of how the adaptation
works.

There's the code, which is the final word on what we're doing at
any given time.

The short story is that we're using Nesterov's dual averaging to
estimate the step sizes based on the samples in the warmup, then
fixing the step sizes for sampling after warmup. Then it's just
a matter of whether we fit a single step size or one per
dimension.

- Bob

messages.author: 1004dd6f66bb10c3
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Stan's approach for hierarchical models
parts:
Quick correction on the last point—we're doing dual averaging (which
is where the "da" in "hmc_da" comes from) to estimate the global step
size, and setting the _relative_ per-variable step sizes proportional
to (a moving estimate of) their relative standard deviations.

Matt
